summary: This experimental memo describes a simple means to associate arbitrary text strings with names, using the Domain Name System to store attributes that DNS does not otherwise define.

eli5.summary: DNS usually stores addresses. This paper shows how to also use it as a notice board where you can pin short notes about a name.

questions: how to extend dns with custom attributes
subtitle: Using DNS TXT records to store arbitrary text attributes alongside domain names.

tldr.problem: The Domain Name System is designed to store only predefined types of information like IP addresses and mail servers. There is no standard way to attach arbitrary text attributes to domain names.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1464 proposes using DNS TXT resource records with a simple format: the attribute name, an equals sign, and the value, all encoded in a TXT record string.
tldr.outcome: This allows applications to store custom attributes in DNS without modifying DNS server implementations, since TXT records are a standard feature.

today: RFC 1464 remains Experimental. While TXT records are a standard DNS feature, this particular use pattern for arbitrary attributes never saw widespread adoption as a standard practice, though TXT records are commonly used for other purposes like SPF and DKIM records.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 1464 describes a simple method to store arbitrary text attributes alongside domain names using the Domain Name System. While DNS is generally used to store predefined information such as IP addresses or mail exchanger names, this memo shows how to extend DNS to hold any attribute that an application needs, without requiring changes to existing DNS implementations.

The approach uses the TXT resource record, a feature that already exists in DNS and is defined in RFC 1035. By encoding attribute names and values into TXT records, applications gain a scalable, distributed way to attach metadata to domain names.
sections.eli5: DNS is a big phone book for the internet. This idea lets you write extra notes next to a name without breaking the phone book.

sections.title: The Attribute Format
sections.content:
An attribute is stored in a TXT record using a simple syntax: the attribute name, followed by an equals sign, followed by the value. For example, printer=lpr5 or favorite drink=orange juice.

Attribute names are case-insensitive and accept any printable ASCII character. If an equals sign appears in the name itself, it must be quoted with a backtick. The value is everything after the first unquoted equals sign, so it can contain equals signs without quoting.

The DNS server returns the attribute with all whitespace preserved; applications decide how to interpret it. When looking up attributes, the system ignores TXT records that have no unquoted equals sign or that start with an equals sign.
sections.eli5: The format is simple: write the thing you want to know, an equals sign, and the answer. Like a label on a jar: contents=sugar.

sections.title: Using Attributes
sections.content:
Applications access attributes through the standard DNS resolver library, though a specialized library routine would make the task easier. Such a routine might provide a function like getattributebyname() that takes the domain name and attribute name, queries DNS for the TXT record, and returns the value with all quoting characters removed.

The memo notes that attribute name registration could be established to ensure interoperability and avoid naming conflicts, but does not propose a specific mechanism for it.
sections.eli5: Programs ask DNS for a note about a domain, and DNS gives back the answer. You could have a library that makes this easy, like a getattributebyname function.
